clue.text: Withdraw from competition, having a slight injury

definitions.meaning: to pull a horse or player out of an event before it starts
a minor graze or nick on the skin

explanation.surface: An athlete pulls out of an event after picking up a minor knock.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are standard senses of one word: a sporting verb for pulling out, and a noun for a small graze.

clue.text: Oracle is upset near the top side of lake

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the word over, so it reads from the bottom up

parts.note: by means near, as in stand by me

indicators.note: the top side of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: An upset oracle on the shore by a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibyl was a prophetess in the ancient world, a woman who delivered oracles.

clue.text: Cheese for girl in bed? On the contrary

indicators.note: in suggests one piece going inside another
on the contrary reverses the relation just stated, so the bed goes in the girl instead

parts.note: Rita is a girl's name
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Is this cheese meant for a girl in bed? No, the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Ricotta is a soft white Italian whey cheese.

clue.text: Man and dog associated with jug

definitions.meaning: Punch and Judy's dog bears this name
a pottery jug shaped like a seated man in a tricorn hat

explanation.surface: A man and his dog connected with a jug.
explanation.walkthrough: Three closely linked definitions. Punch and Judy is the traditional British seaside puppet show.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a man's name, the name of Punch's dog, and the jug shaped like a stout drinker.

clue.text: London Taxi: sorry horse (grey): in a race, nobbled

parts.note: a hack is a worn-out or poor-quality horse

indicators.note: a nobbled racehorse has been tampered with, so these letters are interfered with and reordered

explanation.surface: A poor grey horse doped in a race, set beside a London cab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nobbled' rearranges GREY and IN A RACE into NEYCARRIAGE. To nobble is British slang for drugging a racehorse.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the official name for a licensed black cab, from the horse-drawn hire carriages of old.

clue.text: Sheltered area where diesel is spilt at end of lane

indicators.note: fuel that is spilt runs everywhere, so these letters are scattered into a new order
the end of a word is its final letter, here taken from lane

explanation.surface: A fuel spill at the end of a country lane, hinting at a hazard spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is spilt' rearranges DIESEL into LEESID; 'end of' adds the last letter of 'lane'.
explanation.definitionFit: The side of a ship or hill away from the wind is the protected side, so it is a sheltered area.

clue.text: Anthem offering trade-offs with hymnal, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the letters might form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: An anthem produced by compromise and a hymn book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges TRADEOFFS and HYMNAL together.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Welsh national anthem, Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau in Welsh.

clue.text: Exam — this one makes twelve

definitions.meaning: a test once sat by British children at about age eleven
read as a sum: ... one, gives twelve

explanation.surface: A test, and a puzzle about arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: The old British exam deciding grammar-school places; the second reading takes the hyphen as a plus sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The exam sat in the last year of primary school in England, selecting pupils for grammar schools.

clue.text: King under threat turns chicken …

indicators.note: turns means the letters change round into a new order

explanation.surface: A king facing danger loses his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King under threat' is the chess sense, not a frightened monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, a king attacked by an enemy piece is said to be checked.

clue.text: … early stone implements working the soil

indicators.note: working the soil churns it, so these letters are turned over into a new order

explanation.surface: Ancient stone tools used for tilling the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Eoliths are crudely chipped flints once thought to be the earliest human tools.

clue.text: Could be rasher returning no cab, it seems

parts.note: read the answer as an instruction: the word after 'back' read backwards spells the clue words no cab, so the answer describes returning them

explanation.surface: A taxi-less traveller heading home, with a rasher thrown in as a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: take the answer as wordplay, BACK telling you to read BACON backwards, and you get the clue's 'no cab'. 'it seems' admits the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Back bacon is a cut from the pig's loin, sliced into rashers; 'could be' marks a rasher as one example of it.

clue.text: Former church leader's beginning to be superior

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, here from leader's

explanation.surface: An ex-church leader setting out to show superiority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'church leader' looks like one idea, but the two words split: CE for church, then 'leader's beginning' gives L.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to outdo others or stand out, which is a straight synonym for being superior.

clue.text: Clumsy American baulks at first jump

indicators.note: to baulk is to refuse a hurdle, so the word stalls at its first letter and loses it

parts.note: klutz is American slang for a clumsy person

explanation.surface: An awkward American skater balks at the first leap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baulks at first' drops the first letter K from KLUTZ.
explanation.definitionFit: A lutz is a figure-skating jump, taking off from the back outside edge of one skate.

clue.text: Rambling around Corinth, seen topless

indicators.note: around suggests the letters are turned about and moved around into a new order
topless means the word seen has its top, its first letter, removed

explanation.surface: A traveller wanders about Corinth, spotted without a shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' and 'around' look like scene-setting for the shirtless wanderer, but 'topless' cuts the first letter of 'seen' and 'around' shuffles the lot, leaving EEN to join the city's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rambling speech wanders without a clear thread, so it is muddled and lacking logical connection.

clue.text: Sheet anchor?

parts.note: a sheet anchor is a ship's spare anchor, but here the sheet is bed linen on a washing line and the anchor holds it there

explanation.surface: A nautical term for a ship's emergency anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden or plastic clip holds washing such as bedsheets fast to the line.

clue.text: Mariner finally leaves golf spectators' boat

indicators.note: leaves means departs, so a letter goes out of the spectators' word

parts.note: the crowd following play at a golf tournament is called the gallery

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of mariner

explanation.surface: A sailor walks away from the golf crowd to board a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mariner finally' is R, which 'leaves' GALLERY.
explanation.definitionFit: A galley is a long low ship rowed by oars, used in the ancient and medieval Mediterranean.

clue.text: Medical officer bags Aussie owls

parts.note: a poke is a bag or sack, as in a pig in a poke

explanation.surface: An army doctor bags a few Australian owls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags' looks like a verb but is the plural noun: pokes are sacks.
explanation.definitionFit: The mopoke, or boobook, is a small Australian owl named for its call.

clue.text: Egyptian city's stone home in highway that's not deserted

indicators.note: in places the home inside the highway
D is the dictionary abbreviation for deserted, and 'not' says that letter is dropped

parts.note: a road is a highway
a sett is a badger's home

explanation.surface: Pointing out a famous inscribed stone at a house on a busy road.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the dictionary abbreviation for deserted, so 'not deserted' drops it. The 'stone' belongs to the surface only: the Rosetta Stone was found there.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosetta (Rashid) is a port city in the Nile Delta, where the famous decoding stone was found in 1799.

clue.text: Shipping area, which is proverbially steady on everything

indicators.note: in a down clue, on puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: the saying is steady as a rock
all means everything

explanation.surface: A sea area noted for being reliably calm.
explanation.walkthrough: It is one of the sea areas of the BBC Shipping Forecast, a British radio weather bulletin for sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Rockall is an islet in the North Atlantic that gives its name to a Shipping Forecast sea area.

clue.text: Boy at practice session getting lines!

parts.note: a son is a boy
in cricket, the nets are a practice session in netted lanes

explanation.surface: A boy at cricket practice is given lines as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket nets are netted practice lanes. 'lines' as school punishment misleads: these are lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonnets are fourteen-line poems, so they are poetic lines; the exclamation mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Flying Gulf Air, one missed out having to use economy

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: describing someone obliged to economise

indicators.note: flying suggests the letters are tossed about into a new order
missed out means a letter is left out of the airline name

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A traveller on the Gulf Air flight missed the upgrade and was stuck in economy class.
explanation.walkthrough: Gulf Air is an airline of Bahrain. 'missed out' removes I from GULFAIR; 'Flying' rearranges GULFAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrifty person spends little and saves, which is what economy means here, not the cheap seats.

clue.text: Old lady's maid is a sizeable American, one needing leading liposuctionist

parts.note: big means sizeable
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: leading points to the first letter of liposuctionist

explanation.surface: A large American lady's maid needs a cosmetic surgeon.
explanation.definitionFit: An abigail is an old word for a lady's maid, from a character in Beaumont and Fletcher's play The Scornful Lady.

clue.text: Rewrote scene or act? Bless!

indicators.note: a rewrite redrafts text, so these letters are reorganised into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A playwright rewrote a scene or a whole act, and a weary 'Bless!' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To bless is to make holy by a religious rite, the sense a priest uses for dedicating bread or a church.

clue.text: Some conservatoire backing debauchery

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the selected letters are read right to left
some of a word means just part of its letters

explanation.surface: Part of a music college supports wild living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes TOIR from conservatoire and 'backing' turns it round. Chambers gives wild revelry and debauchery as a sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sense of the word is wild revelry and loose living, as in the phrase riotous living.

clue.text: Tutor rearranged piano quintet

indicators.note: rearranged means the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A music tutor reorganises a piece for piano and strings.
explanation.definitionFit: Schubert's Piano Quintet in A major is known by the nickname of the fish, after the song it varies.

clue.text: Regularly taking out cloisonné cat

indicators.note: regularly taking out means picking every other letter from the word

explanation.surface: Removing pieces from an enamelled ornament of a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: The lion is the big cat of the African savanna.

clue.text: Man the pumps regularly, having finished the lot

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken from the phrase

explanation.surface: A ship's crew keep the pumps going steadily until the job is done.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat everything up is to finish all of one's food, here in past tense to match 'having finished'.

clue.text: Oceanarium, not posh, spilt coffee

indicators.note: spilt suggests letters scattered out of their order
not means the letter for posh is left out

parts.note: U stands for upper class, so posh

explanation.surface: At a downmarket aquarium someone knocks over a cup of coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not posh' removes U from OCEANARIUM; 'spilt' rearranges OCEANARIM.
explanation.definitionFit: An Americano is an espresso diluted with hot water, a common café drink.

clue.text: Pasta course — dip into it!

indicators.note: into says the dip goes inside the course

parts.note: a lane is a course, as in a swimming lane
to sag is to dip or droop

explanation.surface: A pasta course arrives and the diner is urged to dig in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' and 'dip' both want to be about food, but they are LANE and SAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is a type of pasta in flat sheets, also the baked dish layered from them.

clue.text: Vest — and what finishes it off

definitions.meaning: the garment's word itself ends in one lone T

explanation.surface: Laying out a vest and the finishing touch for an outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' is the vest: the word ends with one T, and 'single T' is the answer split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn as underwear or by athletes.
